items.body: An economy uses money balance worth Rs 150 to make transactions worth Rs 600 per month. The velocity of circulation of money is:

excerpts.text:
where, T is the total value of (nominal) transactions in the economy
over unit period and k is a positive fraction.
The two-person economy described above can be looked at from another
angle. You may perhaps find it surprising that the economy uses money
balance worth only Rs 100 for making transactions worth Rs 200 per month.
The answer to this riddle is simple – each rupee is changing hands twice a
month. On the first day, it is being transferred from the employer’s pocket
to that of the worker and sometime during the month, it is passing from the
worker’s hand to the employer’s. The number of times a unit of money
changes hands during the unit period is called the velocity of circulation
of money. In the above example, it is 2, inverse of half – the ratio of money
balance and the value of transactions. Thus, in general, we may rewrite
equation (3.1) in the following form
1

items.proposed_explanation: Velocity of circulation is the number of times a unit of money changes hands in the period, the inverse of the ratio of money balance to the value of transactions. It equals 600/150 = 5.

frozen_blind.source_explanation: Per F19, velocity of circulation is the inverse of the ratio of money balance to value of transactions, so V = 600/150 = 4. 0.25 is the uninverted ratio; 3 and 5 match no computation.

items.body: Government spending on domestic goods rises in an open economy where a proportion of the induced increase in consumption is spent on imported goods. Compared with a closed economy in which all induced consumption is spent on domestic goods, the autonomous expenditure multiplier in this open economy is:

options.text: Larger, because imported goods add to domestic income at each round
Unchanged, because only the change in autonomous expenditure matters
Smaller, because the induced effect on demand for domestic goods is smaller
Smaller or larger depending on the size of the government spending

excerpts.text:
up of the economy can be explained with reference to our previous discussion of
the multiplier process (Chapter 4). A change in autonomous expenditures, for
instance a change in government spending, will have a direct effect on income and
an induced effect on consumption with a further effect on income. With an mpc
greater than zero, a proportion of the induced effect on consumption will be a demand
for foreign, not domestic goods. Therefore, the induced effect on demand for domestic
goods, and hence on domestic income, will be smaller. The increase in imports per
unit of income constitutes an additional leakage from the circular flow of domestic
income at each round of the multiplier process and reduces the value of the
autonomous expenditure multiplier.

items.proposed_explanation: With a positive mpc, part of the induced consumption becomes demand for foreign, not domestic, goods. So the induced effect on domestic income is smaller, and imports per unit of income are an additional leakage at each round that reduces the value of the multiplier. It is therefore not larger or unchanged, and nothing in the stem or excerpt links the size of spending to the direction of the change.

frozen_blind.source_explanation: F25: with a positive import propensity, part of the induced consumption goes to foreign goods, an additional leakage at each round, so induced domestic demand and the multiplier are smaller. A is wrong since imports leak out; B contradicts F25; D is wrong because the multiplier does not depend on the size of spending.

items.body: A person invests Rs 2,00,000 in her family business. The alternatives she could have chosen were: keeping the money in a house-safe (zero return), depositing it in bank-1 at 10 per cent interest per year, or depositing it in bank-2 at 5 per cent interest per year. She can use the money in only one of these ways. The opportunity cost per year of investing in the family business is:

options.text: Rs 0

excerpts.chapter: Theory of Firms under Perfect Competition
excerpts.text:
this money, you can either keep it in the house-safe which will give you zero
return or you can deposit it in either bank-1 or bank-2 in which case you get
an interest at the rate of 10 per cent or 5 per cent respectively. So the maximum
benefit that you may get from other alternative activities is the interest from
the bank-1. But this opportunity will no longer be there once you invest the
money in your family business. The opportunity cost of investing the money
in your family business is therefore the amount of forgone interest from the
bank-1.

items.proposed_explanation: The maximum benefit from the other alternatives is the interest from bank-1, and the opportunity cost of the family business is that forgone interest. 10 per cent of Rs 2,00,000 is Rs 20,000. Bank-2 gives only Rs 10,000, which is not the best alternative; the safe gives zero; and since the alternatives are either/or, their returns are not added to Rs 30,000.

frozen_blind.source_explanation: F33: opportunity cost is the forgone interest from the best alternative, bank-1: 10% of Rs 2,00,000 = Rs 20,000. Rs 10,000 uses bank-2, Rs 30,000 adds alternatives that are mutually exclusive, and Rs 0 uses the safe.

items.body: Government spending rises by Rs 100 crore and the mpc is 0.8. By how much does equilibrium income rise?

options.text: Rs 100 crore
Rs 400 crore
Rs 500 crore
Rs 80 crore

excerpts.text:
up of the economy can be explained with reference to our previous discussion of
the multiplier process (Chapter 4). A change in autonomous expenditures, for
instance a change in government spending, will have a direct effect on income and
an induced effect on consumption with a further effect on income. With an mpc
greater than zero, a proportion of the induced effect on consumption will be a demand
for foreign, not domestic goods. Therefore, the induced effect on demand for domestic
goods, and hence on domestic income, will be smaller. The increase in imports per
unit of income constitutes an additional leakage from the circular flow of domestic
income at each round of the multiplier process and reduces the value of the
autonomous expenditure multiplier.

where YD = disposable income.
We note that taxes lower disposable income and consumption. For instance,
if one earns Rs 1 lakh and has to pay Rs 10,000 in taxes, she has the same
disposable income as someone who earns Rs 90,000 but pays no taxes. The
definition of aggregate demand augmented to include the government will be
—
AD = C + c(Y – T + TR ) + I + G (5.2)

items.proposed_explanation: The multiplier is 1/(1 - mpc) = 1/0.2 = 5, so income rises by 5 x 100 = Rs 500 crore. Rs 100 crore ignores the induced rounds, Rs 400 crore is the induced part only, and Rs 80 crore is mpc x 100.

frozen_blind.source_explanation: With only mpc given, the multiplier is 1/(1-0.8) = 5, so income rises by Rs 500 crore. F25/F23 note that imports and taxes act as extra leakages, but none are specified. Rs 400 crore is mpc/(1-mpc), Rs 100 crore ignores induced rounds, and Rs 80 crore is only the first induced step.

items.body: A wheat farmer in a perfectly competitive market is a price-taking firm and sells every unit at the market price of Rs 40 per quintal. If she sells one more quintal, her marginal revenue from that extra quintal is:

options.text: Less than Rs 40, because she must lower the price to sell the extra quintal
Rs 0, because the extra quintal is sold at the same price as the earlier ones
Rs 40, because the extra unit is sold at the market price
Rs 40 multiplied by her total output, because all units are sold at that price

excerpts.chapter: Theory of Firms under Perfect Competition
excerpts.text:
= p
Thus, for the perfectly competitive firm, MR=AR=p
In other words, for a price-taking firm, marginal revenue equals the market
price.
Setting the algebra aside, the intuition for this result is quite simple. When a
firm increases its output by one unit, this extra unit is sold at the market price.
Hence, the firm’s increase in total revenue from the one-unit output expansion –
that is, MR – is precisely the market price.

items.proposed_explanation: For a price-taking firm, the extra unit is sold at the market price, so marginal revenue is precisely the market price, i.e. MR = AR = p = Rs 40. The firm does not need to lower its price, so MR is not below Rs 40. The extra quintal adds Rs 40 to revenue, so MR is not zero or Rs 40 times total output.

frozen_blind.source_explanation: F34: for a price-taking firm the extra unit is sold at the market price, so MR = p = Rs 40. A describes a price-making firm, B is unsupported, D gives total revenue.

items.body: At an output of 4 units, a firm has a total fixed cost of Rs 80 and a total variable cost of Rs 120. Using SAC = AVC + AFC, what is the short run average cost (SAC) at 4 units?

options.text: Rs 30
Rs 50
Rs 200
Rs 20

excerpts.text:
Clearly,
SAC = AVC + AFC (3.10)
In Table 3.3, we get the AFC-column by dividing the values of the second
column by the corresponding values of the first column. Similarly, we get the
AVC-column by dividing the values of the third column by the corresponding
values of the first column. At zero level of output, both AFC and AVC are
undefined. For the first unit of output, AFC is Rs 20 and AVC is Rs 10. Adding
them, we get the SAC equal to Rs 30.
The short run marginal cost (SMC) is defined as the change in total cost
per unit of change in output

items.proposed_explanation: AFC is obtained by dividing fixed cost by output (80/4 = Rs 20) and AVC by dividing variable cost by output (120/4 = Rs 30). Since SAC = AVC + AFC, SAC = 30 + 20 = Rs 50. Rs 30 is only AVC and Rs 20 is only AFC; Rs 200 is the total of 80 + 120, not a per-unit cost.

frozen_blind.source_explanation: By F32, SAC = AVC + AFC = 30 + 20 = Rs 50, equal to TC/4 = 200/4. Rs 30 and Rs 20 are single components, and Rs 200 is total cost.

items.body: A farmer's four-acre farm needs only two workers and himself to carry out its operations through the year. He employs five workers along with his wife and children, and everyone on the farm works throughout the year. This situation is best described as:

options.text: Disguised unemployment, because more persons are employed than the farm actually needs
Open unemployment, because the extra persons have no work at all and are seeking jobs
Seasonal unemployment, because farm work is available only in some months of the year
Full employment, because every person on the farm is working

excerpts.text:
described in the first
paragraph of this section is called open
unemployment. Economists call
unemployment prevailing in Indian farms
as disguised unemployment. What is
disguised unemployment? Suppose a
farmer has four acres of land and he
actually needs only two workers and
himself to carry out various operations
on his farm in a year, but if he employs
five workers and his family members
such as his wife and children, this
situation is known as disguised
unemployment. One study conducted in
the late 1950s showed about one-third
of agriculture workers in India as
disguisedly unemployed.
You may have noticed that many
people migrate to an urban area, pick
up a job and stay there for some time,
but come back to their home villages
as soon as the rainy season begins.
Why do they do so? This is because
work in agriculture is seasonal; there
are no employment opportunities in the
village for all months in the year. When
there is no work to do on farms, people
go to urban areas and look for jobs.

items.proposed_explanation: The farm needs only two workers and the farmer, yet employs five workers plus family members; this situation is known as disguised unemployment. It is not open unemployment since the stem says everyone on the farm works, and not seasonal since they work throughout the year. Full employment is contradicted by the excerpt, which labels this very situation disguised unemployment.

frozen_blind.source_explanation: F11 defines this exact situation as disguised unemployment: more persons are working than the farm needs. B is wrong since the extra persons are working, C because everyone works all year, D because surplus labour exists despite everyone being occupied.

items.body: The price of a complementary good of coffee rises, other things remaining the same. The demand curve for coffee will:

options.text: Shift rightward
Shift leftward
Remain unchanged, with only a movement along the same curve
Become perfectly elastic

excerpts.text:
hence, there is a shift in the demand curve. If there is an increase in the price of
a substitute good, the demand curve shifts rightward. On the other hand, if
there is an increase in the price of a complementary good, the demand curve
shifts leftward.
The demand curve can also shift due to a change in the tastes and preferences
of the consumer. If the consumer’s preferences change in favour of a good, the
demand curve for such a good shifts rightward. On the other hand, the demand
curve shifts leftward due to an unfavourable change in the preferences of the
consumer. The demand curve for ice-creams, for example, is likely to shift
rightward in the summer because of preference for ice-creams goes up in
summer. Revelation of the fact that cold-drinks might be injurious to health can
adversely affect preferences for cold-drinks. This is likely to result in a leftward
shift in the demand curve for cold-drinks.

items.proposed_explanation: When the price of a complementary good increases, the demand curve for the good shifts rightward, so coffee demand rises at every price. The other options are not supported.

frozen_blind.source_explanation: F29: an increase in the price of a complementary good shifts the demand curve leftward. A is the substitute case, C confuses a shift with a movement along the curve, D has no basis.

items.body: In a production process all inputs are doubled and output rises to 2.5 times its earlier level. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The production function exhibits increasing returns to scale
Output has increased by a larger proportion than inputs
The production function exhibits constant returns to scale
The production function exhibits decreasing returns to scale

excerpts.text:
Decreasing Returns to Scale (DRS) holds when a proportional increase in
all inputs results in an increase in output by a smaller proportion.
For example, suppose in a production process, all inputs get doubled.
As a result, if the output gets doubled, the production function exhibits CRS.
If output is less than doubled, then DRS holds, and if it is more than doubled,
then IRS holds.

items.proposed_explanation: Output (2.5 times) has grown by a larger proportion than inputs (2 times), which is the case of more than doubled output and hence increasing returns to scale. Constant returns would need output exactly doubled and decreasing returns would need it less than doubled.

frozen_blind.source_explanation: By F31, output more than doubling when inputs double means increasing returns to scale, so A is true. B merely restates this (2.5x versus 2x) and is also true, so two options are correct. C and D are contradicted by F31.
